📌 Crypto Options: Buying Insurance on Price Moves

Main Points
⏺ Crypto options give you the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an asset at a set price
⏺ They’re used for hedging, income, and directional bets with defined risk
⏺ This post explains how options differ from simple spot or futures trades

1️⃣ Calls & Puts — call options give you the right to buy at a strike price, puts give you the right to sell at a strike price.
2️⃣ Premium — you pay an upfront fee (premium) for that right; if you don’t use it, the option can expire worthless.
3️⃣ Hedging — options can cap downside (buying puts) or lock in upside (selling calls against a position).
4️⃣ DeFi Options — on-chain protocols let you buy, sell, and structure options with smart contracts instead of brokers.
5️⃣ Defined Risk — unlike leveraged futures, your max loss as an option buyer is the premium you paid.

Final Thoughts

Crypto options turn “all or nothing” price bets into flexible strategies — more tools to shape your risk instead of just hoping the chart goes your way.

How much would Bitcoin need to be worth to match the real purchasing power of $1 million from different eras?

The equivalent of $1 million in 2023 purchasing power would require Bitcoin to reach roughly $1.5 million per BTC (around 2036), while matching the purchasing power of $1 million in 1983 would require a price of approximately $6 million per BTC (around 2043).

Crypto speak: Bull trap

A “bull trap” is a market analysis term that refers to a cryptocurrency’s price action that feigns an impending long-term upward (bullish) trend when, in reality, it’s secretly a short-term correction with more downward pressure.

In other words, if you see a crypto’s price pumping and immediately rush to buy it, congratulations, there’s a strong chance you’re entering a bull trap, and your coin is about to get cheaper 🙃

📌 Zcash sets July 28 hard fork to seal Orchard after critical bug 

⚠️ Zcash founder Zooko Wilcox has explained how the network’s July 28 Ironwood hard fork will address uncertainty around a critical flaw in the Orchard shielded pool. The upgrade will not identify or freeze individual counterfeit coins. Instead, it will seal the old pool and limit how much ZEC can leave. 

🔖 Ironwood, also known as NU6.3, is scheduled to activate at block 3,428,143 on July 28. The upgrade will retire the current Orchard pool and introduce a new shielded pool based on the corrected circuit. According to Zcash’s official Ironwood user update, users will no longer be able to send or receive ZEC inside the old Orchard pool after activation. Funds can leave only through the turnstile, which prevents more ZEC from exiting than legitimately entered.

⭐️ The Zcash team said it believes the flaw was “unlikely to have been exploited,” but users cannot independently prove no counterfeit ZEC was created. Ironwood aims to trap any excess value inside the old pool rather than allow it to enter wider circulation. Security researcher Taylor Hornby discovered the Orchard flaw on May 29 while auditing the shielded system. The bug could have allowed an attacker to create counterfeit ZEC inside Orchard without leaving an obvious public record.

🧨 The New Middle East™: Israel as a Side Note

Netanyahu sold Washington a simple fantasy: Israel smashes the “Shiite axis,” America crowns it regional hub, and the new order is built around Jerusalem. 

He delivered the demolition part — Iran’s nuclear program wrecked, Khamenei dead, Hezbollah leadership gutted — and then watched the political sequel roll out without him.

While he was declaring “objectives achieved,” Trump was cutting deals Israel wasn’t even allowed to read. The April ceasefire with Iran? Brokered in Islamabad, not Jerusalem. 

The June memorandum? Named for Pakistan’s capital, negotiated through Pakistan and Qatar, with no Israelis at the table. By July, the pattern was open: Trump lifts sanctions on Turkey and talks F‑35s over Netanyahu’s objections, then signs a 30‑year civil nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia that opens a legal path to enrichment and demands no recognition of Israel in return.

That Saudi deal is sold as “one step closer to a bomb.” It isn’t — there is no plant, no study, no enriched fuel — but it kills three old bargains that once held the region together. 

The tech‑for‑recognition trade is dead: Biden’s offer was reactors and guarantees in exchange for normalization with Israel; Trump split the package and handed Riyadh the nuclear half for free. The “gold standard” — US nuclear technology only if you renounce enrichment and accept intrusive inspections — becomes optional the moment the Saudis get softer terms than the UAE. 

And the unwritten rule that big US decisions in the region require Israeli sign‑off evaporates when Turkey’s sanctions and Saudi enrichment go through against explicit objections from Jerusalem.

Everyone else uses the opening. Riyadh buys status and insurance: a possible enrichment plant, more room to defy Washington on airspace and oil, and a quiet test of how far a “partner” can drift before the US pays to keep it. 

Pakistan sells what it really has — mediation between Washington and Tehran, the ability to host memoranda and ceasefires — instead of mythical warheads. Turkey accumulates capability from Russia, the West, and East Asia at once, building Akkuyu with Rosatom, shopping for new plants from Seoul, Beijing, and Washington, and sitting under unacknowledged US nuclear weapons at Incirlik.

Israel, meanwhile, discovers it has become both indispensable and irrelevant. Militarily, it helped break Iran’s program and the proxy network that constrained it for a generation. Politically, the road to Washington no longer runs through it. 

The Saudis can get nuclear status without saying the word “Israel.” Turkey can get sanctions relief and a path to F‑35s while publicly clashing with Netanyahu. Pakistan can redefine the war’s endgame without inviting Jerusalem to the room.

The war against Iran didn’t end the region’s nuclear question; it changed the casting. The Saudis are buying status, the Pakistanis are selling brokerage, the Turks are quietly building competence. Status can be revoked. Brokerage can be sidelined. 

Competence sticks. Israel still has a lot to offer — tech, intelligence, hard power — but its new role is nastier: a powerful player that can’t set the rules and can’t block the deals.

The New Middle East is under construction. Israel is still on the map — just no longer at the center of it.
